claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA is single-phase BCC.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA has high density.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA has insufficient room-temperature ductility.
Adding 2-5 at.% Al can trigger B2 ordering without destabilizing the primary BCC matrix.
Minor Al addition will precipitate a B2-ordered intermetallic phase with a NiAl-type structure.
The B2 precipitates will form a reticulated network along grain boundaries and within matrix grains.
Annealing will promote formation of the proposed secondary intermetallic network.
The ordered B2 network will act as a physical barrier to crack propagation.
The B2 network will arrest cracks through crack deflection and bridging.
The matrix will retain sufficient plasticity in the presence of the B2 network.
Dual-phase high-entropy alloys can simultaneously increase yield strength and uniform ductility.
Solid-solution hardening typically reduces ductility.
Al addition will simultaneously improve yield strength and uniform ductility relative to the unalloyed baseline under room-temperature compression.
The Al-added alloy's density will increase by less than 5%.
The lower atomic mass of Al relative to Hf and Zr causes a marginal increase in alloy density.
The ordered B2 phase is locally denser than the surrounding material.
The unalloyed baseline has high strength.
The unalloyed baseline fails brittly at room temperature because it lacks crack-arresting mechanisms.
A continuous intermetallic skeleton formed above a critical Al concentration would cause catastrophic embrittlement.
The proposed B2 phase is stable during room-temperature compression.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts a density increase, but the stated rationale is substitution with low-atomic-mass Al, which ordinarily points toward a density decrease rather than an increase. No composition, molar-volume, or phase-fraction calculation resolves this inconsistency.
